canberra.title: Voluntary redundancies will harm Canberrans ‘in the worst possible way’: union
canberra.snippet: Warnings are already sounding that Canberra’s most vulnerable are going to be even worse off if voluntary redundancies are taken up...
canberra.content:
CPSU ACT regional secretary Maddy Northam (front) warned voluntary redundancies in the Health and Community Services Directorate would adversely impact vulnerable Canberrans and the wider community. Photo: CPSU.

Warnings are already sounding that Canberra’s most vulnerable are going to be even worse off if voluntary redundancies are taken up at the Health and Community Services Directorate (HCSD).

The ACT Government agency announced on Thursday (1 October) that 65 positions would go across its more than 1500-strong workforce.

“[This is] to ensure that we are able to continue operating within our available budget,” HCSD Director-General Kareena Arthy said.

“We will be assessing applications carefully to ensure the directorate retains the workforce knowledge and capability to ensure we meet our important statutory obligations.

“We’re taking this action now to ensure we are on a sustainable financial footing while we continue to provide essential services for Canberrans.”

Ms Arthy wouldn’t confirm which areas within the directorate would be targeted by the program, but said it would be open to all staff.

“I have no expectation at the moment about where we will have the EOIs come from,” she said.

Some executives are excluded from the program.

HCSD’s budget papers foreshadowed the directorate was 45 full-time equivalent positions in excess, which is how it reached the 65 figure.

While forced redundancies have been ruled out, management offered no clarity on what happens if voluntary departure targets fall short.

But Ms Arthy had this message for people accessing HCSD’s services.

“People who are going through the child protection system and getting domestic violence support … their programs and their support services will remain the same,” she said.

“We’re undertaking a process where we’re going to be assessing every application on its merits, and we’ll be looking at the impacts on service delivery, impacts on workload, before we make any decision about whether to accept [an EOI].”

“One of our core criteria of the assessment is looking at the impact of service delivery capability and we will be taking that into account when making the final decision.”

Community and Public Sector Union ACT regional secretary Maddy Northam said any job cuts would affect some of Canberra’s most vulnerable people who rely on these public sector workers.

“We’re talking about youth workers, child and youth protection workers, Child and Family Centre workers supporting Thriving Kids, and Housing ACT staff,” she said.

“The consequences of this decision will ripple through Canberra in the worst possible way, with our members worried that if these jobs cuts go ahead, the consequences for the community could be dire.”

Ms Northam said she was deeply concerned about the impact this program would have on workers who remained at the directorate.

“The Barr Government must reverse this decision and start investing in public sector work so our members can continue to deliver services that are vital to the health and wellbeing of Canberran communities,” she said.

Bimberi Youth Centre workers undertook strike action as negotiations on pay and conditions continue. Photo: CPSU.

One service under the HCSD is the Bimberi Youth Justice Centre.

Workers took strike action on Tuesday (29 September) as they sought recognition and payment for unpaid time.

Ms Northam said some workers were losing hours of pay a week.

“Bimberi youth workers are required to complete essential security and equipment checks before they can reach their posts, yet they are not paid for that time,” she said.

“These workers are simply asking to be paid for the work their employer requires them to do.”

After 12 months of bargaining, the government proposed a 10-minute allowance, later upping the offer to 20 minutes.

The union has also requested a meal allowance, a condition that has thus far been rejected.

The Pegasus Economics report into the 2026-27 budget outlined that employee expenses were the “largest single component” of ACT Government expenditure, representing about 40 per cent of the total cost.

It warned voluntary redundancies would cost the government money in the short term.

“Only one new measure [in the budget papers] – a fund to assist agencies with voluntary redundancies – explicitly addresses whole-of-government expenditure reform,” it stated.

“That measure is forecast to add to expenses in the first three years and only generate savings in 2029-30.”

Opposition leader Mark Parton has questioned why public service staff should be the ones expected to take a package for the HCSD to remain within a budget it couldn’t control.

“This is yet more upheaval before Christmas,” he said.

“Machinery-of-government changes, hiring pauses and redundancies have already hit the [public] service. Labor restructures, spends on consultants and new programs, [and] then cuts the people who deliver the work.

“Voluntary redundancy does not make a staffing cut any less real. Canberrans will feel it in longer waits and thinner services.”

The ACT Greens have called on the government to release a full breakdown of the roles to be affected and an explanation on how the changes would impact essential community service delivery.

The EOIs opened today and will close on 8 November.

Offers are expected to be made in early to mid-December.

canberra.title: Anika Wells named in Time’s top 100 rising stars list
canberra.snippet: Federal Communications Minister Anika Wells has made Time magazine and for all the right reasons, featuring in the prestigious journal’s ...
canberra.content:
Communications Minister Anika Wells features in this year’s edition of Time magazine’s 100 Next list. Photo: Facebook.

Federal Communications Minister Anika Wells has made Time magazine and for all the right reasons, featuring in the prestigious journal’s list of the world’s most influential rising stars.

The Time 100 Next 2026 is the latest list of global players the magazine describes as “leaders who are shaping the future”.

Since the annual list launched in 2019, it has gained widespread recognition as a who’s who of people to watch and learn from.

Ms Wells is featured in the newly released edition for her leadership in driving Australia’s social media ban for under-16s and for continuing to stand up to global tech giants over their manipulation of algorithm feeds.

Former Labor Prime Minister Julia Gillard penned the testimonial accompanying a photo of Ms Wells in the Time 100 Next edition.

She describes the minister as courageous and trailblazing.

“As the world grapples with the extraordinary power of social media and the increasingly pervasive role it plays, Anika Wells has emerged as one of the most significant voices in a growing global movement to reframe the relationship between technology and the well-being of our children,” the testimonial says.

“As Australia’s Communications Minister, she has championed world-leading reforms to protect young people from the harms of social media.

“Even in the face of intense opposition from some of the world’s largest tech companies, she remains steadfast.

“Guided by the vital objective of protecting our children and their future, she has overseen the introduction of online safety measures – including rules supporting Australia’s social media minimum-age policy – that are designed to better protect young people.

“It has placed Australia at the centre of conversation on online safety, accountability, and the responsibilities of Big Tech.

“Future generations will look back on her landmark changes as courageous and trail-blazing.”

Actress Yerin Ha and pop singer Troye Sivan were other Australians included in the list.

Sivan was included under the ‘Advocates’ section, with a testimonial from pop princess Kylie Minogue.

“Fans recognise something very personal in him. They see magnified versions of themselves, complete with life’s challenges, wonders, and aha moments,” she wrote.

“To them, he’s a hero and confidante. Of course, Troye is also a dazzling north star of gay achievement. With each new record, he steps deeper into his true self, and we are here to celebrate his evolution.

“As a fellow Melburnian, I have loved watching his ascent to global renown. We so would’ve been friends in school.

“He’s a ‘beaut’ of Australia, beamed out to the world. Troye doesn’t just make pop music to love. He makes pop music to believe in.”

Ha was listed under the ‘Phenoms’ section of the list and received a testimonial from fellow Bridgerton actress Nicola Coughlan (also of Derry Girls fame).

“And when they found Yerin Ha, they really found an absolute diamond. Leading Bridgerton is a wonderful but intense experience,” she wrote.

“You feel the pressure because people love the show so much, but she never wilted. She dealt with it with such grace. She is someone who is so talented, and so brilliant at what she does.”

Ms Wells featured in the ‘Leaders’ section of the Time 100 Next 2026 list.

The minister’s social media ban for under-16s came into effect on 10 December 2025, resulting in the removal or deactivation of more than 4.7 million underage accounts.

It was a world-first move that has led other international jurisdictions to consider doing the same.

But some social media platforms are still under fire for not fully embracing the new laws, allowing children and young teenagers to find ways around them.

The Federal Government is now also seeking to mandate an opt-out provision so social media users can choose not to get constant algorithm feeds tailored to their online conversations and use.

canberra.title: Bright lights and a stacked entertainment lineup headline another huge year for NightFest
canberra.snippet: NightFest is finally back for 2026, with the popular springtime event expected to attract tens of thousands of visitors to Commonwealth P...
canberra.content:
NightFest is back at Commonwealth Park with new displays and a stacked musical lineup. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

NightFest is finally back for 2026, with the popular springtime event expected to attract tens of thousands of visitors to Commonwealth Park over the next four nights.

This year’s festival sees the return of the light-up Ferris wheel at the heart of Commonwealth Park, as well as installations from the world-famous production company MandyLights.

Visitors can discover countless new displays this year, including a light-up walk bridge, a neon garden, unique pond artworks, and even a section where you choose the colour of the lights.

The lights aren’t the only thing bringing the park to life; nightly shows include Drag Bingo, a Fire Extravaganza, and a bunch of street performers, all adding to the nighttime festivities.

This year’s NightFest will also have one of the strongest musical lineups in the event’s near 18-year history. Split Enz frontman Tim Finn headlines opening night, with ARIA winners Busby Marou and Christine Anu taking to the stage on Friday.

Saturday night will see one of Australia’s favourite new-generation rock bands, Pacific Avenue, rock Commonwealth Park before the legendary Temper Trap wrap up NightFest on Sunday.

NightFest truly displays Floriade in a new light. Photos: Jarryd Rowley.

Sit back and relax in the Neon Garden.

A view from the top of the Feris Wheel.

Even the ponds at Commonwealth Park are bubbling with excitement.

Events ACT executive branch manager Ross Triffitt said NightFest has only grown year on year by creating an exciting way to enjoy Floriade.

“NightFest is all about creating an exciting evening experience during Floriade. The flowers are the centrepiece during the day, but all the lighting, the installations and the entertainment transform the park once it goes dark,” he said.

“The lighting displays this year really interact with the garden beds, so the different themes of the beds have got different lighting treatments.

“They’re all going to be lit up and transformed. There was a real focus on having a walk-through and interactive experience for visitors.”

You get to decide what colour the lights should be. Photos: Jarryd Rowley.

Enjoy a dance across the brilliant light bridge display.

A stop at one of the many kitchens and beer gardens is well worth it.

Cap off the night at NightFest's centre stage!

Mr Triffitt said he is excited for visitors to enjoy the stacked entertainment lineup.

“This year’s festival definitely has the strongest lineup of entertainment we’ve had over the full four nights,” he said,

“In terms of music, Tim Finn, Christine Anu, Busby Marou, Pacific Avenue and The Temper Trap are all extremely talented.

“We also have a lot of really special local musicians who really add to the fantastic schedule of entertainment we have over the course of NightFest.”

Over 30,000 people are expected to attend across the four nights, with Mr Triffitt projecting over $4 million to be injected into the ACT economy from NightFest alone.

“Last year, the whole Floriade festival contributed about $56.7 million in visitor spend coming into the territory, and a total economic spend of $71.5 million,” he said.

“Night Fest contributed about $4 million of that in terms of visitor spend. Close to 50 per cent of our audience are from interstate, so it’s really about Canberra owning the season of spring nationally and attracting international visitors as well.

“Floriade, along with NightFest, just continues to grow. We’ve now got over 100 local businesses and local community groups getting involved in some way or another.

“This time of year really brings not just Commonwealth Park to life but the entirety of Canberra.”

Tickets for all four nights of NightFest can be purchased on the Floriade website.

canberra.title: Tax Office accused of hypocrisy for refusing credit cards while business has to absorb costs
canberra.snippet: The Australian Taxation Office is being accused of hypocrisy for deciding not to accept credit card payments now that the surcharge ban h...
canberra.content:
From today businesses can no longer pass on surcharges for card payments, so the ATO will refuse to accept credit cards after 30 November. Photo: File.

The Australian Taxation Office is being accused of hypocrisy for deciding not to accept credit card payments now that the surcharge ban has come into effect.

The card payment surcharge ban has kicked in from today (1 October) and means business transactions can no longer add a separate surcharge because a customer pays by card.

The surcharge ban covers EFTPOS, Visa and Mastercard and includes credit, debit and prepaid cards.

The new rule was introduced following a Reserve Bank of Australia’s Review of Merchant Card Payment Costs and Surcharging, which found that removing the surcharges would support a more efficient and competitive payments system.

The ATO, however, has responded to the ban by bluntly refusing to accept credit card payments after 30 November.

It says that as a government agency, it would not be appropriate for the cost of credit card merchant fees to be “transferred to the community”.

“The ATO recognises that some taxpayers currently rely on credit card payments to manage their tax payments and understands this change may require some adjustments,” it said in a statement.

“The ATO is committed to helping taxpayers transition to alternative payment methods and will continue to support those experiencing financial hardship or other circumstances that make it difficult to meet their obligations.”

The Tax Office is writing directly to those who currently have a payment plan linked to a credit card to explain the changes and the steps they need to take.

Taxpayers with a direct debit arrangement linked to a credit card will need to update their payment method before their next instalment due after 30 November to ensure compliance with their payment plan.

About 2.3 per cent of tax payments were made with credit cards in 2024–25.

The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry has described the ATO’s move as “utter hypocrisy” because it won’t absorb the costs like businesses now have to.

ACCI CEO Andrew McKellar said the chamber was also “deeply disappointed” the ATO decided to wait until the surcharge ban came into effect before making it public it will no longer accept credit card payments as a result of it.

“It is utter hypocrisy that the ATO, a government agency, refuses to absorb the costs of extending payment options to credit cards, yet expects small businesses across the country to absorb them because of a ban the government is implementing today,” Mr McKellar said.

“When decisions like this are deliberately hidden until the last moment, it is little wonder so many small businesses are angry at the government.

“Surcharging was never a revenue tool for small businesses, it was just a way to transparently recover merchant service fees.

“This ban is causing dread across small businesses who are bracing for increased costs at the terminal, reprinting menus and putting up prices today.”

ACCI has been steadfastly opposed to the ban, saying the blanket approach treats surcharging as the problem instead of “tackling the real issue” – high and opaque merchant card payment costs that businesses must pay to banks and other payment providers.

ACCI’s 2024 submission on the change highlighted that in hospitality more than three-quarters of businesses applied a surcharge.

All surveyed businesses applied a rate under 2 per cent purely to cover merchant service fees, and none applied surcharges for profit.

Mr McKellar said this reflected broader practice across the small business community, which represented more than 97 per cent of all Australian businesses.

“Small businesses did not surcharge because they wanted to. They surcharged because the payment system has a cost for every transaction,” he said.

“Small businesses are now having to absorb the cost of transactions at the very time interest rates are going up, and homegrown inflation continues to push up prices.”

Treasurer Jim Chalmers, however, has hailed the end of what he said are “pesky” card charges for customers.

He said it would ease cost-of-living pressure, saving customers a total of $1.6 billion a year.

“What you see on the menu [now] is what you pay when you tap your card,” Dr Chalmers said.

“This is about easing the cost of living; this is about the end of those annoying, pesky surcharges that everyone has paid in one way or another.”

The changes only apply to surcharges added because a customer chooses to pay by card.

They do not affect legitimate booking fees, service fees, delivery charges or hospitality surcharges for weekends and public holidays.

australia.title: After a huge and costly glow-up, the largest stage in the southern hemisphere is ready for play
australia.snippet: Two and a half years since closing its doors, Melbourne’s renamed Ian Potter State theatre is back. Don’t be fooled by the fact that it, ...
australia.content:
Two and a half years since closing its doors, Melbourne’s renamed Ian Potter State theatre is back. Don’t be fooled by the fact that it, kind of, looks the same

We are standing on the vast, empty stage of Victoria’s newly refurbished State theatre – days before its official reopening and two and a half years since it closed its doors to the public – as we wait for the curtain to rise. Normally we’d be facing the other direction, but this time we aren’t anticipating what’s on this enormous stage (bigger than four tennis courts, it is the largest in the southern hemisphere), but what’s in the auditorium. Actually, we’ve come to see the auditorium itself, the centrepiece of this first stage in the $1.7bn redevelopment of Arts Centre Melbourne.

Curtain up, and then a kind of hushed bemusement.

Nothing much seems different. The layout is largely the same, the brass and burgundy colour scheme is definitely the same, and most of the improvements and alterations are subtle or out of sight. “Everything you see here might look the same,” says the director of the Arts Centre Melbourne Reimagining Project, Chris King, as if to confirm we aren’t all going mad, “but there are ever so slight differences that make all the difference.”

The 2,000-seat State theatre was designed by Australian actor and designer John Truscott and opened with great fanfare in 1984; 40 years later, it was looking a little tired. It was also unfit for purpose, due to structural limitations in the design and contemporary code violations. A beloved and vital Melbourne theatre – its closure has seen pressure placed on the city’s other performance spaces, notably the Regent – it is home to major companies such as the Australian Ballet and Opera Australia. Any alterations would be noticed.

The first change worth addressing is the name, which is now officially the Ian Potter State theatre (although convincing Melburnians to adopt the change may prove trickier). Announced without public consultation in 2024, the decision to name yet another Victorian arts institution after an admittedly generous benefactor – this adds to the Ian Potter Centre in Federation Square, and the Potter Museum of Art in Parkville – has rankled many, including a publicly vocal Eddie Perfect who called it “a big fat mistake”.

Hamish Lyon, director of the company hired to oversee the project, NH Architecture, agrees the public are unlikely to embrace its full title, and thinks that’s perfectly fine. “People know it as the State. What [the name change does] is recognise the largest single philanthropic gift to a performing arts centre in the country in history. But for most punters, they’re going to see a show in the State theatre like they have for 40 years.”

One key update that should be universally welcomed is a massive improvement in disability access: excellent seats across all three levels can be easily reached by wheelchair, and accessible seating is now supported by two new lifts. More importantly, these additions feel plush and welcoming rather than utilitarian or ad hoc, an approach people with mobility issues are usually made to endure in public spaces. It’s necessary change, overdue.

Two generous new aisles in the stalls now meet a central walkway, forming an apron that should improve audience flow. Air flow has also greatly improved, with audience comfort being “a major factor in everything we tried to achieve,” King says. “Previously, the air conditioning used to come from above. About 12 or 15 minutes into every show, there would be this cold air dump, the system’s way of dealing with 2,000 bodies.” Now the air comes from below.

Carpets have been replaced with magnificent blackbutt timber that elevates the whole auditorium and helps with the acoustics. Sound quality, which was notoriously patchy, has been significantly improved; even the backs of the seats, designed by Italian furniture manufacturer Poltrona Frau, play a role in augmenting sound. “It’s an amazing art, acoustics,” Lyon says. “A mix of high science and black magic art.”

Most of the improvements are technical and therefore invisible, from a complete redesign of the sound system – which King says “used to be stuck on the wall” – to a new performance lighting system. Perhaps the most noticeable alterations are the added front two rows in the balcony, and the exquisite gold leafing on the ceilings.

Walking through the new theatre from the stalls to the balcony, it’s clear that an enormous amount of love and attention has been poured into the task of making it look like nothing’s been done. This refurbishment has deliberately leant on the softly, softly approach, vastly improving amenity without disturbing the building’s original aesthetic.

If the teams who’ve worked on it seem nervous that enough changes are visible to the naked eye to justify in the public’s mind the eye-watering cost – this stage of the redevelopment included a state government injection of $241m – they should take comfort in the experience of ARM Architecture, who redeveloped Hamer Hall in 2012. That project was simultaneously bold and conservative, and Victorians embraced the refit with massive enthusiasm.

The grand opening to the public will coincide with a First Nations-led concert called Gugu Dindi Gunyah (Many Rivers, One Home), and a three-day series of performances featuring over 100 Victorian artists titled Housewarming, all totally free. The acoustics will be fully tested by Opera Australia’s Wagner Gala in mid-October, and Australian Ballet will return with The Nutcracker before Opera Australia’s My Fair Lady takes over for summer.

Melbourne has its theatrical crown jewel back, shinier than ever and ready for play.

australia.title: ‘Politics can be brutal’: Sarah Hanson-Young speaks out about divisions within Greens
australia.snippet: Greens sources say the relationship between new leader David Shoebridge and runner-up Mehreen Faruqi is seriously strained Get our breaki...
australia.content:
Sarah Hanson-Young has spoken out about major divisions in the Greens party room, offering support to newly elected leader David Shoebridge and describing politics as “brutal”.

The South Australian senator contested Wednesday’s leadership ballot, finishing behind Shoebridge and outgoing deputy leader, Mehreen Faruqi.

Former leader Larissa Waters shocked colleagues by resigning on Monday, over serious health concerns.

Hanson-Young was eliminated after the first ballot with only two votes.

“God, politics can be brutal,” she said in a video posted to social media, after a bush walk with her husband on Thursday.

“Friendships made and lost, but it takes all types. We all care so deeply about the future of this country and the future of the planet.”

Hanson-Young said it would take a huge effort to defeat One Nation and its leader, Pauline Hanson, and warned “the radical right” would wreck the country if it wins power.

“Australians deserve a optimistic, caring, and defiant progressive force, and I won’t be backing down,” she said.

“I’m sorry we couldn’t pull it off this time, but buckle up, because we’ve got a lot of work to do.”

Her comments come a day after Faruqi criticised her colleagues for electing Shoebridge and demanded the party’s rank-and-file members be given a say in future leadership elections.

Greens sources say Shoebridge and Faruqi’s working relationship is seriously strained.

The New South Wales senator said she planned to pursue bold politics and radical action to fight “against genocide, wars, surging fascism” and climate change, working from outside “the constraints of the leadership team”.

In an interview with Guardian Australia’s Australian Politics podcast on Thursday, Shoebridge said he and the newly elected deputy, Victorian senator Steph Hodgins-May, had received a strong endorsement from their colleagues.

Shoebridge said he could work with Faruqi, praising her for effective community engagement.

“I have huge respect for Mehreen and the work that she does. And, acknowledging as well, the attacks that she gets and the way she keeps turning up proudly and strongly, taking the case forward in the face of all of those attacks.

“That is something that I have immense respect for and gratitude for.”

Shoebridge said Greens MPs wanted Faruqi to continue her engagement with voters and Greens members.

“Sometimes you want to be part of the leadership team. Sometimes you want to be out connecting with the community in a different way.

“We’re all human beings and we all know how in the moment how we can best contribute to the project.

“I take Mehreen at her word that that’s how she thinks she can best connect with the community, how she can best connect with the project. And she has my 100% support to go on being the amazing Greens senator that we’ve all seen.”

He committed to giving rank and file party members the right to vote in leadership elections in time for the next scheduled contest, due to take place immediately after the next federal election.

A party plebiscite in 2020 saw 62% of Greens members support a party-wide vote for leader, but the move fell short of a required two-thirds majority.

australia.title: Australian couple on plane diverted after flydubai pilot’s alleged attack on co-pilot
australia.snippet: Two people from Sydney were on board flight to Tel Aviv that was dramatically diverted to Saudi Arabia after one pilot allegedly stabbed ...
australia.content:
Two Australian citizens onboard a flight to Tel Aviv that was diverted after one of the pilots allegedly stabbed the other in an attack are “safe,” the foreign minister confirmed.

The passengers are a Jewish couple from Sydney, the Israeli embassy in Australia confirmed to the Guardian on Thursday.

No further details were provided.

The flydubai aircraft was travelling from the United Arab Emirates to Israel when it was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

In a post on social media, Penny Wong thanked the “heroes” for thwarting the attack.

“Relieved to confirm at least two Australians who were on the Flydubai flight to Israel are safe – thanks to the heroes who thwarted the attack and helped bring the passengers to safety,” she wrote.

“We’re thinking of those injured and hope for their full recovery.”

One of the pilots, whom Israeli officials said was an Omani citizen, is accused of stabbing his co-pilot. During the alleged attack, the plane plunged about 17,000 feet in just two minutes.

Passenger Yaniv Hayoun later recounted how he and other passengers heard screaming and felt pressure as the plane dived before forcing their way into the cockpit and finding the attacker at the instrument panel.

“I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during a meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel. “He was trying to destroy the instruments to disable the plane.”

Israel’s ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, said the incident reminded him of the 11 September attacks.

“You have here a very special incident, and due to the real heroism of some people on board, they were saved.”

Newman said heightened security alerts had been issued after the attack.

“It just shows that … those that hate Israel also hate the peace.

“It’s an attempt to hit at the peace itself, at the Abraham Accords, and the relationships which Israel does have with Arab and Muslim countries.”

The Abraham Accords normalised relations between the UAE and Israel in 2020.

Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said it was too early to tell who was ultimately behind the incident.

There are about 12,000 Australian citizens living in Israel and 25,000 in the UAE.

australia.title: First home buyers with big loans among those most at risk of falling into negative equity, RBA warns
australia.snippet: Central bank estimates fewer than one in 100 borrowers owe more on their home than its worth Follow our Australia news live blog for late...
australia.content:
The Reserve Bank says households are well placed to weather the twin storm of rising interest rates and falling property prices, although it says recent borrowers who have taken out big loans are most at risk of falling into negative equity.

Despite a deepening property price slump concentrated in Sydney and Melbourne, the RBA’s analysis suggested that fewer than one in 100 borrowers owe more on their home than it’s worth.

Those included first home buyers who took advantage of the government’s 5% home guarantee scheme, the RBA said, although evidence suggested that the share of these borrowers falling behind on their payments remained “contained”.

The RBA also estimated that even a 20% property price crash would only push about 5% of mortgages into negative equity – a testament to the fact most homeowners have enjoyed significant value gains over the years.

The RBA also found that most indebted homeowners were coping with higher borrowing costs and wages that were not keeping up with the recent burst of inflation.

The analysis showed a little under 2% of mortgaged homeowners didn’t have enough income to cover essentials and the mortgage payments, similar to six months earlier. That share would stay roughly the same “for some time”, based on the RBA’s forecasts, and well below the recent peak of nearly 5% in 2024.

“While some households continue to experience hardship, the estimated share of mortgagors in severe financial stress or in arrears has, so far, remained low, supported by the strong labour market and mortgagors’ savings and equity buffers,” the report said.

“Negative equity is insufficient to trigger default if borrowers remain able to service their loans, which remains the case for the vast majority of these households.”

The central bank’s latest financial stability review – a biannual assessment of the financial system – said the “threats to global financial stability continue to mount”.

The governor of the RBA, Michele Bullock, last month said AI could be a bubble, and that “all central banks are a little bit worried about that”.

This concern was reiterated in the financial stability review, which said high valuations in global corporate debt and share markets meant they were vulnerable to a “disorderly” correction.

“One possible trigger could be a shift in sentiment towards the AI investment boom, which is increasingly fuelled by expectations of sustained rapid earnings growth and a debt-financing cycle that is becoming more opaque and circular,” the report said.

“Australia is unlikely to be immune” from the impact, it said.

Alongside the huge sums being invested in artificial intelligence, two ongoing conflicts – in the Middle East and Ukraine – alongside “intensifying strategic competition among major powers” underscored these threats, the RBA said.

The RBA also warned of the rising risk of cyber-attacks, potentially facilitated by AI, and a sudden sell-off in global bond markets.

“These external factors are the most prominent threats to financial stability in Australia.”

australia.title: ‘Where illegal ebikes go to die’: first bikes seized under new laws in NSW crushed
australia.snippet: Major Sydney hospital also warns recent injuries from ebikes include fractures, internal bleeding, as well as ‘perforation of certain org...
australia.content:
The first illegal ebikes seized under new laws have been crushed in New South Wales, as a major Sydney hospital has warned of a spike in trauma injuries driven by those riding under the influence.

The NSW government crushed 23 ebikes at a wrecking yard in western Sydney on Thursday, turning them into scrap metal. NSW police are assessing applications for the return of an additional 13 bikes seized during a joint operation with Transport for NSW in the northern beaches in September.

The NSW transport minister, John Graham, told reporters onsite on Thursday “this isn’t a scene from Mad Max. This is where illegal ebikes go to die.”

Graham said tough new laws were necessary “because of some of the bad behaviour we’ve seen … on our state’s streets, on the golf courses in Sydney suburbs, even on the Sydney Harbour Bridge”.

On the same day, St Vincent’s hospital released figures that showed a 22% spike in legal and illegal ebike injuries, with 42% of those injuries triggering a trauma response and the majority being injured while riding under the influence of alcohol or drugs, riding too fast or without a helmet.

It found 361 patients presented to the hospital for ebike injuries between January and July, compared with 296 presentations during the same period last year.

Dr Ed Lewis, acting head of rehabilitation medicine, told reporters injuries included fractures, internal bleeding, as well as the “perforation of certain organs”. He said they often included brain injuries from severe head trauma, “as well as milder knocks, like a concussion, which can still have long-term repercussions for patients”.

Lewis told Guardian Australia that those contemplating riding an ebike home while intoxicated “need to have a plan B or a backup solution”.

“The message that we want to say to people is: enjoy using ebikes, but respect what they are. Respect that they are fast. Wear a helmet and just don’t ride impaired.”

Graham said the government was concerned by the number of injuries, but it was “important to keep it in context”.

“The number of ebike injuries is still low compared to cars … but is rising,” he said. “If you’re not wearing a helmet, you are dicing with danger.”

He stepped aside to allow a giant metal claw pick up a tangle of ebikes, cracking frames in half and popping tyres. They were loaded into a conveyor belt before being crushed and shredded. Graham said batteries had been removed for safe disposal and recycling beforehand.

Under powers which came into effect in August, police and transport officers can seize bikes not restricted to 25km/h, whose maximum speed while not pedalling does not exceed 6km/h, and maximum continuous power of 500 watts, due to reduce to 250 watts in March 2029.

The government says the bikes crushed include one capable of speeds of more than 90km/h seized from a 14-year-old, a food delivery bike, and bikes with speed restriction settings that had been tampered with.

The 36 ebikes seized so far represent a fraction of the estimated 760,000 in the state. The changes were prompted by a surge in injuries and high-profile incidents, including one in which about 40 ebikes swarmed the Sydney Harbour Bridge in February. An expert review on implementing an age limit of between 12 and 16 was due to report back to the government in June.

The NSW premier, Chris Minns, appearing on the debut of Kyle Sandilands Live in August, said the government was “examining an … age limit of 12”, but hadn’t finalised the details.

On Thursday, Graham would not say if the premier had revealed the planned age limit. “I want to discuss this with my colleagues and also with the public,” he said.

world.title: Trump administration diverts human rights funds to push far-right agenda abroad
world.snippet: Support such as for white Afrikaners and anti-communism reveals how US is redefining what qualifies as human rights With hours left befor...
world.content:
With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a huge $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilizational norms”.

On Wednesday, the state department obligated the funds to the grantees hours before the deadline despite congressional concerns and requests not to do so, according to a source familiar with the negotiations. The state department declined to comment on questions from the Guardian specifically on whether it had obligated the funds and had “blown” holds from Congress due to concerns about the money’s use.

Critics have focused on 43 awards of a combined $176.9m that will bolster rightwing and conservative causes around the world while probably angering US allies over interference in internal politics. The Guardian has seen a sample of the controversial grants, which make up most of the $205m in funding that Congress has appropriated for the entire Human Rights and Democracy Fund (HRDF).

Sources with knowledge of the grant process have told the Guardian that the awards were personally lobbied for by members of the Trump administration, and reflect interests that include JD Vance’s warnings of the collapse of traditional western values in Europe and Stephen Miller’s push against immigration and to support white minorities in countries like South Africa.

“The story for me is the high-level – including White House-directed – attention on these programs,” said a person familiar with the discussions over the democracy awards. “These awards have been briefed at the highest levels of the department and have buy-in from the White House.”

The proposed awards represent a significant shift in US support for dissidents, human rights defenders and civil society groups under authoritarian governments. The new slate includes projects in wealthy nations, and those focused on opposition to regulation, Brexit, immigration, anti-communism, Christian protection and opposition to “gender ideology”, offering a window into how the Trump administration is redefining what qualifies as human rights and merits tens of millions of dollars in US foreign assistance.

“Congress appropriated money for the democracy fund on a bipartisan basis to support defenders of human rights, to assist victims of human rights violations and to instead promote the growth of democracy abroad,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the US Senate committee on foreign relations.

“The Trump administration’s proposals would use taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies. This is a waste of resources and undermines United States values and relations with democratic partners, including allies in Europe.”

A Democratic congressional aide said Shaheen had maintained 10 holds on $22m of awards focusing on Brazil, South Africa, Nigeria, and the promotion of a rightwing ideology in the United Kingdom and in Europe. According to the aide, secretary of state Marco Rubio had personally signed a memo to disregard the holds and obligate the funds.

The largest award, of $40m, was directed to a consortium led by the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation (VOC), an anti-communist non-profit that has received far smaller grants in the past. A state department vetting document seen by the Guardian records $96,997 in previous contracts in the last five years between the foundation and the department, all in the 2022 fiscal year, and notes that it had been vetted in 2019 in connection with tickets to the foundation’s gala. The vetting document also identifies Andrew Bremberg, a former Trump White House domestic policy adviser and US ambassador to the UN European office, as a “senior leader” of the foundation.

In July, ProPublica reported that Samuel Samson, a 27-year-old deputy assistant secretary overseeing the new grants, was linked to senior members of VOC through his studies at the Christian conservative Hillsdale College graduate program. (A state department official then told the outlet that the relationship had nothing to do with the grant).

Samson has described the US and Europe as partners in a shared civilizational struggle. Samson toured Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia last December – all countries that were floated to receive a $2m grant to counter migration weaponized by Russia and Belarus – and criticized NGOs that previous administrations had worked with for promoting what he called radical concepts, including gender theory and DEI.

The state department did not comment on individual grants but said the programs were still in “active deliberation”, that awardees would meet guidelines for federal grants, and that all programming would undergo a “standard and rigorous vetting process by grant professionals”.

“Our programming in Europe aims to support our European allies in defending those rights and principles, along with their civilizational self-confidence and sovereignty from those who seek to undermine them,” a state department official said. “The national security strategy highlights our priorities in Europe, which includes advancing political liberty, promoting free speech, and collaborating with European partners to jointly support European revitalization and civilizational self-confidence.”

Under the legislation authorizing the fund, the money must be assigned by 30 September, the end of the fiscal year, when unobligated funds typically lapse.

The Guardian first reported that Trump officials had drawn up no-bid grants aimed at rightwing and anti-immigration causes in Europe. ProPublica similarly reported that there were at least a dozen no-bid grants earmarked for rightwing projects.

The document now shows how much of the fund the plan takes up, and which awards have since been dropped.

A $1m award titled “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court. The Trump administration sanctioned the Brazilian justice Alexandre de Moraes last year after lobbying by Eduardo Bolsonaro, son of the former president.

A program titled “Promoting Western Civilization Allies” would be limited to implementers who do not subscribe to “ideologically weaponized accounts of human rights, such as gender ideology”, according to the document, and will receive $2m. It names possible recipients in Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and the Balkans with “anti-communist” and “natural rights” approaches.

One award was allocated to document “democratic backsliding” in Europe tied to “mass and illegal migration” and legislation by “supra-national entities”, while a $1m journalism consortium would push back against designations of “trusted” media outlets. The list also includes $2m for early-warning networks protecting Christians in Nigeria.

And a $3m no-bid award would go to the Jobs Foundation, a UK group run by Matthew Elliott, who led the Vote Leave campaign. The grant, titled “Countering Overregulation to Advance American Investment”, would promote a “common good capitalism index” and pro-business policy, including how the foundation promoted Brexit as a chance to cut the UK’s climate regulations.

The document also shows that a proposed $5m no-bid grant to the Free Speech Union, the British group founded by Toby Young, has been marked “withdrawn”. When the award was first reported in July, Young said the group had never applied for or received US government money (though Trump officials had reportedly met with the group during a European tour late last year).

The grant would have paid the group to campaign against online safety and hate speech laws, including Britain’s Online Safety Act, a law passed under the Conservatives in 2023. Meant to protect children from harmful content and enforced by Ofcom, it has age-verification rules – which took effect last year – that have drawn constant criticism from the Trump administration, which cast them as censorship.

The Free Speech Union is the second British group to drop off the list. A $7m no-bid award to 878, a thinktank whose stated missions include restoring Judeo-Christian culture and “ending mass migration and deporting illegal immigrants”, was abandoned in July after pushback from Congress. It was founded by Jacob Rees-Mogg, who served as Brexit opportunities minister and business secretary before losing his seat at the 2024 election, and now presents on GB News.

The British awards would have sent $15m in US taxpayer money to groups run by two sitting Conservative peers and a former cabinet minister, regarding issues including online safety law to immigration.

world.title: South African leader urges men to speak up on gender-based violence after series of killings
world.snippet: President announces measures amid anger at authorities over recent murders of women South Africa’s president has called on men to take mo...
world.content:
South Africa’s president has called on men to take more responsibility for violence against women as he announced measures to tackle the problem, amid anger at authorities over a recent wave of murders.

Cyril Ramaphosa acknowledged that not enough had been done to protect women. He said police would be reviewing unsolved murders, attempted murders and serious sexual offences against women and children, as well as producing a funded plan to reduce the forensic backlog for such cases, both within 60 days.

In a televised speech on Tuesday night, the president said local governments would have five months to address issues that compromised women’s safety, from broken streetlights to overgrown public spaces and abandoned buildings. He added that he had tasked five ministers to come up with a plan within 60 days to reduce alcohol-fuelled violence.

“Alcohol does not cause gender-based violence and it can never excuse it. Responsibility always lies with the perpetrator,” Ramaphosa said. “But harmful alcohol use is a significant aggravating factor in interpersonal violence and it must be addressed as part of our wider prevention effort.

“Women should not have to live in fear because government has failed to repair a light, clear a public space, process evidence or enforce a law.”

South Africa has been gripped by grief and fury after the discovery of 11 women’s bodies dumped across Ekurhuleni, the municipality adjoining Johannesburg to the east, since 15 July. Eight of the women were found in the last three weeks, including Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo, who was discovered on 12 September after she went missing when she went for a run after work.

Ramaphosa said suspects had been arrested in connection with three of the killings and that the other cases would not be left to go cold. He added that police had not found evidence that a serial killer was responsible for all 11 killings, but that all possibilities were still being investigated.

He directly addressed South African men, urging them to challenge relatives, friends and colleagues who harassed, humiliated or abused women. “It is time for good men to stop being silent men,” he said.

“For too long, gender-based violence has been treated as a woman’s problem to solve. Women march, the women of our country organise, they speak out, they protest, they confront and they comfort survivors,” Ramaphosa said.

“Women change their routes home. Avoid going out at night and warn one another about dangerous places and dangerous men. We have placed the burden of male violence on women. That must change.”

Activists expressed their frustration that solid policy actions had not been taken years ago and scepticism that the measures Ramaphosa had announced would work.

Shenilla Mohamed, the executive director of Amnesty International South Africa, said: “These are not new issues and as a country we have been talking about ways to tackle the high numbers of [gender-based violence and femicide], especially since 2019 when women took to the streets to protest, and yet here we are again in the face of continued attacks against women.

“Amnesty International South Africa also notes the timelines put in place by the president, but this will only mean something if it results in action, and if there are consequences for inaction.”

Mpiwa Mangwiro-Tsanga and Bafana Khumalo, of Sonke Gender Justice, an NGO, said: “Our concern … is that the response remains heavily weighted towards what happens after violence has already occurred.”

They added: “Investigating unresolved cases, processing forensic evidence and repairing unsafe public spaces are necessary, but they do not constitute a comprehensive prevention strategy. It is concerning that the president is asking municipalities to do what is actually their mandate and yet they do not deliver on these.”

world.title: Burundi agrees to receive ‘third-country’ migrant deportees from US
world.snippet: Burundi joins several other African nations in accepting people deported under Trump’s hardline policy Burundi has agreed to join a clutc...
world.content:
Burundi has agreed to join a clutch of ⁠other African nations in receiving migrants from other countries deported from the US under ⁠Donald Trump’s hardline ⁠immigration ​policy.

However, Burundi will only accept those not accused of crime or terrorism links, said ⁠Nancy Ninette Mutoni, a spokesperson for the country’s president, Évariste Ndayishimiye. Tuesday’s announcement gave no details of numbers, timing or financial ⁠details.

Washington has sent so-called “third-country deportees” to about half ​a dozen African nations ‌as well as many other countries, often where they have no ties, have never been and find themselves detained indefinitely, under opaque deals ‌that Senate Democrats say have cost tens of millions of ‌dollars.

In many cases, deportees had secured legal protections from immigration courts in the US against repatriation. But rights groups say the third-country deals allow the US to circumvent those protections.

Mutoni said preparations were under way to arrange accommodation, ‌living conditions and integration into local communities in Burundi. “Receiving them requires serious planning – where they will stay, what they ​will eat and how they will live alongside the local population,” she said.

“If they choose to join Burundian citizens and make a valuable contribution to national development, the law ⁠will be respected,” she said, regarding potential citizenship.

Burundi aimed ​to both ​strengthen diplomatic relations and provide ​hospitality to people in need, the spokesperson ​added.

The US ‌state department ​did not ​immediately respond to requests for comment while a spokesperson for the Burundi foreign ministry said details of the agreement were not yet available.

world.title: DRC politician beaten to death after radio appearance about Ebola outbreak
world.snippet: Marie-Celestin Karondwa was attacked on Sunday after promoting measures to prevent spread of disease, his party says A senior member of t...
world.content:
A senior member of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s ruling party was beaten to death on Sunday after appearing on a radio programme to raise awareness about the Ebola outbreak, a party representative has said.

Marie-Celestin Karondwa, the acting president of the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) party’s federal executive committee in Butembo, a new hotspot for the outbreak, was attacked after taking part in a ​radio show during which he ‌promoted prevention measures for the disease, ‌the UDPS federation in the city said in a statement, Reuters reported.

The party ‌said the attackers beat Karondwa, stole his belongings and set his house on fire, and that he later died from his injuries.

It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack, how many people were involved or what motivated it, but the party said Karondwa was “an innocent victim for having defended ‌the party’s position on the existence of the Ebola virus disease … and the threat it poses to ​the population”.

Karondwa’s death comes after a series of attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres that experts say are fuelled by rumours and misinformation about the disease and distrust of health responders.

The incidents have included violence, riots and property damage and the disruption of essential services. On Saturday, ​armed men attacked a hand-washing ​checkpoint in the nearby Beni territory, killing at least one ​person and wounding ‌several others, a ​local civil ​society group reported.

First identified in 1976 in what is now the DRC, Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.

The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected 8,067 people and killed 3,901, according to data from the DRC’s health ministry.

Cases of the disease have been confirmed in seven provinces.

The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in the DRC’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.

Data from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention shows the current outbreak has outpaced the west African one.

Last month, the World Health Organization warned it was on track to surpass the west Africa outbreak. Experts say the spread of the disease has been intensified by several factors, including conflict, aid cuts and the attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres.

Reuters contributed to this report

world.title: At least 27 dead after two mass shootings in South Africa, police say
world.snippet: Seventeen people killed near Johannesburg in suspected ‘illegal goldmining turf war’, as 10 killed in separate incident at barbecue venue...
world.content:
Two separate mass shootings near South Africa’s two biggest cities killed at least 27 people, as the country grapples with one of the world’s highest murder rates amid investigations into corruption and criminality within the police.

The South African police service said on Sunday that 17 people were killed on Saturday night when eight suspects armed with AK-47 assault rifles and pistols opened fire at a bar in Wedela township, about 50 miles south-west of central Johannesburg. At least 15 other people sustained gunshot injuries in that attack, police said.

In a separate statement, police said 10 people had been killed in a mass shooting at an entertainment venue selling grilled meat, known as shisanyama, in Lwandle, near Cape Town. Another 11 people were wounded in that shooting. Police said they were searching for multiple suspects, without giving an exact number.

The two attacks happened days after a mass shooting by three gunmen at a house party near the east-coast city of Durban killed 11 people, including a pregnant woman.

No arrests had been made in the two latest mass shootings, police said.

South Africa has struggled with high rates of violent crime for years, but the series of mass shootings this week were shocking even to a country used to some of the highest violent crime rates in the world.

“This ​cannot go on like this,” South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, told local TV news channels. “This is the level of criminality that we must bring down, and our security forces are now going ⁠to continue pulling out all stops.”

Police in the province of Gauteng said on Sunday morning they had launched a manhunt for the unidentified eight suspects in the Johannesburg tavern shooting, with no arrests yet made.

“It is alleged that patrons were drinking inside and outside the tavern when the suspects arrived and opened fire on those outside,” a police spokesperson, Capt Tintswalo Sibeko, said in a statement.

“The suspects then entered the tavern and continued shooting at patrons inside. The suspects were reportedly armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols. They allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles. Two vehicles were also set alight during the incident.”

While many local residents did not want to speak about the shooting, one said that illegal goldminers were active in the area. Gauteng province’s police commissioner, Tommy Mthombeni, told reporters that one of their lines of inquiry was that the shooting was part of a “turf war in terms of illegal mining”.

Illegal miners, known as zama zamas, which means “to take a chance” in Zulu, are usually part of powerful gangs, with multiple mass shooting incidents around Johannesburg blamed on them in recent years.

Mthombeni also said Saturday’s shooting could have been retaliation for another at the same tavern about a month ago.

Western Cape police said they had set up a team led by serious violent crime detectives to investigate the Cape Town shooting, in which the gunmen entered the shinsanyama venue at about 1.46am on Sunday and starting shooting at customers.

“Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities,” the statement said. “Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained … Detectives are hard at work in search of the perpetrators of the shooting incident, with no arrests effected yet. The identities of the deceased persons will be released once their next of kin are informed.”

A police official said that “business jealousy might have been the issue”, citing reports that people had been buying cheaper alcohol elsewhere and then bringing it to the venue to drink.

South Africans are already reeling after the discovery of numerous women’s bodies near Johannesburg’s airport since July, most of which were found in the last few weeks. The killings led to renewed anger about high rates of gender-based violence in the country, and have piled pressure on police and politicians to do more about it.

Alongside this, the Madlanga commission judicial inquiry has been examining allegations of corruption and criminality within the police in televised hearings for the past year.

South Africa had a murder rate of almost 40 per 100,000 people in 2024, according to the UN office on drugs and crime. That was the ninth-highest in the world that year, with only Caribbean countries higher.

In the 12 months to 30 June, more than 22,700 people were murdered in South Africa, according to police data.

Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report
